bone-muscle.title: Bone and muscle
bone-muscle.intro: Without gravity, bones lose mineral and muscles shrink. Watch how crews fight back with about two hours of exercise a day.

items.caption: The interim resistive exercise device (IRED) gave early station crews a way to load their legs and spine with squats and lifts.
Running on the TVIS treadmill, held down by a harness. Impact loading helps protect bone density in the legs and hips.
Treadmill runs are a daily countermeasure: they keep the heart, legs and bones working against a pull that is no longer there.
COLBERT, the station treadmill. Crews log many kilometres on it to preserve fitness and bone.
The ARED lifts real loads without gravity, using vacuum cylinders. It is the main defence against bone and muscle loss on station.
Squats and deadlifts on the ARED load the hips and spine, the bones that lose the most in orbit.
Resistance exercise has to be done with the body strapped in so the force goes into the bones, not the room.
Strength training on the ARED. Exercise time is scheduled into every crew day like any other task.
Crews practise on the ground before flight so the routine is familiar when it counts.
MARES measures how strongly astronauts' joints and muscles can work, to see how spaceflight changes them.

items.caption: Muscle cells grown for a station study of how weightlessness weakens muscle at the cell level.
A plain-language tour of the running, cycling and lifting that keeps crews healthy.

radiation.title: Radiation
radiation.intro: Beyond Earth's magnetic shield, radiation is the hazard with no easy fix. These are the instruments and dummies that measure it.

items.caption: An astronaut works with active dosimeters, small instruments that log the radiation dose a crew receives.
Bubble detectors grow tiny bubbles when neutrons hit them, a simple way to count radiation dose.
A tissue-equivalent dosimeter, built to read dose the way human tissue would absorb it.
HERA, a monitor that tracks radiation levels around the station in real time.
The Matroshka phantom is a human-shaped model packed with detectors, showing how deep radiation reaches inside a body.
A Matroshka phantom set up in the Kibo module, measuring dose at the organs.
Radiation detectors in the Service Module, part of a long-running dose-mapping effort.
The AstroRad vest is designed to shield blood-forming organs during a solar particle event.

items.title: Phantom torso in the Human Research Facility
items.caption: A torso model with dosimeters inside, used to measure how much radiation reaches the organs.
How NASA plans to protect astronauts from solar and cosmic radiation on longer trips.

sleep-isolation.title: Sleep and isolation
sleep-isolation.intro: Sixteen sunrises a day, small cabins and months away from home. Sleep and mood need as much care as muscle.

items.caption: A station sleeping quarters. Each crew member gets a small private booth with a sleeping bag tied to the wall.
Three crew members peek out of their sleeping quarters on Christmas morning. Sleep stays on a fixed schedule even though the sun rises every 90 minutes.
The inside of a crew quarters booth: the quiet, dark place an astronaut uses to sleep.
An astronaut in her sleeping bag in her personal crew quarters. A private space helps with sleep and mood on long missions.

items.title: Skylab astronaut strapped into a sleep restraint
items.caption: On Skylab in 1973, sleep restraints stopped crew drifting off while they slept.
Peggy Whitson at the temporary sleep station set up in the US lab in 2002, before permanent crew quarters.
Music, movies and rest: how crews recharge when home is 250 miles below.
Wristbands record sleep and movement on Artemis II to show how crews adjust to a small cabin.

twins-study.title: Twins Study
twins-study.intro: Scott Kelly spent a year in orbit while his identical twin Mark stayed on Earth. Their differences show what space does to a body.

items.caption: Scott Kelly gives himself a flu shot for the immune-system part of the Twins Study. Mark got the same study on Earth.
Scott and Mark Kelly before launch. Having an identical twin on the ground made this a one-of-a-kind comparison.
The twins pose together at Baikonur before Scott launches on his one-year mission.
Mark Kelly fist-bumps his twin through the glass before launch.
The brothers speak with reporters about the mission. Researchers followed both for blood, genes, gut bacteria and more.
Mark Kelly speaks to his twin by phone while Scott was aboard the station in 2010.
The twins reunited after an earlier flight. Both are astronauts, which made them closely matched test subjects.
Scott Kelly in the station's Node 1, partway through his year in space.

life-support.title: Life support / CO₂
life-support.intro: Every breath adds CO₂ to a sealed cabin. Scrubbers, oxygen makers and water recyclers keep the air safe.

items.caption: Installing the Sabatier system, which turns CO₂ and hydrogen into water and methane so the station recovers more water.
Replacing parts of the CO₂ removal assembly (CDRA) in Node 3. It scrubs carbon dioxide from cabin air.
Scott Kelly and Terry Virts replace a CDRA part, routine upkeep that keeps CO₂ low.
Maintenance on the CDRA in the Japanese module. Crews fix their own air system in orbit.
An astronaut removes a carbon dioxide system part during a repair.
Hydrogen sensor work on the oxygen generator, which splits water to make breathable air.
Swapping a part of the oxygen generation assembly, the machine that makes the station's air.
Checking the water recovery system for leaks. It turns sweat and urine back into drinking water.

items.title: Water recovery and management on the ISS (diagram)
items.caption: A diagram of how water flows through the station's recycling loop.
NASA's life support lab at Marshall, where the next generation of air and water hardware is tested.
How the station's life support system keeps the air breathable and the water clean.
The station now recycles 98% of the water its crew uses.

spacewalks.title: Spacewalks
spacewalks.intro: A spacewalk means hours in a pressurised suit, a long day for the heart, hands and nerves. Here is how crews prepare.

items.caption: Suit hardware being prepared. The spacesuit is a personal spacecraft that supplies oxygen and keeps pressure steady.
An astronaut outside the station on a spacewalk. Hours of suit work tire the hands and shoulders.
Peggy Whitson on a spacewalk. Suits are pressurised, so even gripping a tool takes effort.

items.title: Spacewalk 23 view
items.caption: A view from a spacewalk where a crew member works at the end of a long day outside.
A view during the second spacewalk on the early station stack, 1998.
A shuttle-era spacewalk during the building of the station.
An astronaut gets ready for a spacewalk. Preparing the suit and body is half the job.
Training for spacewalks in the pool, which mimics weightlessness for suited astronauts.
A NASA flight director explains how spacewalks work and what crews go through.
The long process of getting into a suit before stepping outside.
Volunteers live in a pressure chamber to test how the body responds to the pressure changes of a spacewalk.
A virtual reality lab where astronauts rehearse spacewalks.
